unit.title: Attach flexible cables & plugs to electrical machinery appliance and fixtures

summary: This unit teaches you to choose, fit and test flexible cords and plugs on appliances, portable machines and light fittings. You will learn how cords are built and rated, which plug suits which voltage and current in Jamaica, how to prepare and terminate a cord so that it stays safe in use, how to make up extension leads, and how to inspect, test, label and record the work, including the work of trainees you supervise.

blocks.p: A flexible cord and its plug are the parts of an appliance that are bent, pulled, stepped on and plugged in thousands of times. They are also where many shocks and fires start: a cord too thin for its load, an earth that has pulled out, a plug that lets a 110 V tool reach 220 V. Fitting a cord looks simple, and that is why it is often done badly. This unit is for Level 3 trainees who choose the cord and plug, do the calculations, fit and test them, and check the work of others.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Work safely on plug-connected equipment
Unplug and keep control of the plug, discharge capacitors, let hot parts cool, and never work on a connected appliance.
Choose the cord
Work out the current, then pick the number of cores, conductor size, insulation and sheath to suit the appliance and where it is used.
Choose the plug or connector
Match the plug to the appliance's voltage and current and to the outlet, and never defeat the pin pattern.
Prepare and terminate
Strip the sheath and cores without damage, connect each core to the right terminal, leave the earth longest, and clamp the sheath in the cord grip at both ends.
Deal with moulded plugs, cord sets and joins
Replace instead of joining, destroy cut-off plugs, and choose the right detachable cord set.
Make up extension leads
Plug at the supply end, socket at the far end, voltage drop checked, GFCI protection for outdoor use.
Inspect and test
Visual inspection, earth continuity while flexing, insulation resistance and polarity, with the right tests for Class I and Class II.
Label, record and advise
Pass and fail labels, an appliance register, a clear job record, and plain advice to the customer.
Supervise
Open and check trainees' work, correct faults, and set up inspection programmes for a workplace.

ul: Ordinary outlets are **110 V, 50 Hz**; outlets for larger appliances and machines are **220 V**. The plugs and outlets are the North American (NEMA) patterns, and each voltage and current rating has its own blade pattern.

Cord colours vary with where the equipment was made. US-style cords: **black** line, **white** neutral, **green** earth. European-style cords: **brown** line, **blue** neutral, **green-and-yellow** earth. Older British cords: red, black and green. Check, never guess.
Cord sizes may be given in **AWG** (a lower number is a thicker conductor) or in **mm²**.
Sun, salt air, heat and rain are hard on cords. Choose sheaths made for the conditions.

blocks.note: A 110 V appliance on 220 V gets twice its rated voltage and about four times the power in a heating element: it can burn out or catch fire in seconds. The plug pattern is what stops this. Fitting the wrong plug, or using an adaptor that defeats the pattern, removes the protection.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Working safely on cords and plugs

flow: Switch off and unplug
Keep the plug in view, or fit a plug lock-out cover
Wait for hot parts to cool and moving parts to stop
Check for and discharge capacitors
Inspect before you open anything
Work at a clean, dry, well-lit bench

ul: **Unplugged is the isolation.** For plug-connected equipment, pulling the plug and keeping it where you can see it is the safe isolation. If you leave the bench, or the plug is out of sight, fit a lockable plug cover.

**Capacitors.** Machines with motors, and some appliances, have capacitors that hold a charge after unplugging. Measure across the capacitor and discharge it with a proper resistor tool before you touch the terminals. Never short it with a screwdriver.
**Never plug in to 'see if it works'** before the dead tests. At the Centre only the instructor runs equipment, on a protected test bench.
**Tools.** Use a sheath stripper, wire strippers set to the conductor size, side cutters and screwdrivers that fit the screws. Cut away from your body and wear safety glasses: cut strands fly.
**Old cords and cut-off plugs** are destroyed at once (see 'Plugs, connectors and cord sets').

head: Class
How it protects
Cord
rows: Class I
Basic insulation plus an **earthed** metal body: a fault to the body trips the breaker
Three-core, with the earth core connected to the body, and a three-pin plug.
Class II (double insulated; a square inside a square)
Two layers of insulation, or reinforced insulation; **no earth connection**
Two-core, with a two-pin plug. Never add an earth to a Class II appliance.
Class III
Runs at extra-low voltage from a safety transformer or battery
The cord carries only the low voltage; the transformer or charger has its own mains cord.

sections.title: Flexible cords: how they are built and rated

head: Part
What it does
rows: Conductors (cores)
Many fine copper strands, so the cord can bend again and again. Solid building wire work-hardens and cracks when flexed, so it is never used as a cord.
Insulation
Covers each core and carries its colour.
Fillers and binder
Keep a round cord round and stop the cores moving.
Sheath (jacket)
The outer covering. It protects the insulated cores from wear, water, oil, heat and sunlight. It is the part the cord grip must hold.

head: Type (US marking / harmonised marking)
Sheath
Use
rows: Parallel lamp cord (SPT)
Light PVC, two cores side by side
Lamps, radios and other small Class II items indoors. Not for heaters, tools or outdoor use.
Light and ordinary-duty PVC cord (SJT / H05VV-F)
PVC
Office and household appliances indoors: fans, computers, fridges.
Ordinary-duty rubber cord (SJOOW / H05RR-F)
Rubber, oil-resistant in the OO types
Portable tools and appliances that are handled a lot.
Heavy-duty rubber cord (SOOW / H07RN-F)
Thick rubber: resists wear, oil, water and weather
Building sites, workshops, pumps, portable machines, outdoor extension leads.
Heater cord (HPN and similar heat-resistant cords)
Heat-resistant rubber or silicone
Irons, hot plates, toasters, kettles: anywhere the cord can touch hot surfaces.

blocks.p: In US markings, **S** means service cord, **J** junior (300 V, lighter), **T** thermoplastic (PVC), **O** oil-resistant sheath (**OO**: sheath and insulation), **W** rated for weather and water, **P** parallel and **H** heater. In harmonised markings, **05** means 300/500 V and **07** 450/750 V, **V** is PVC, **R** rubber, **N** polychloroprene (neoprene) and **F** flexible.
These are typical ratings for cords with two current-carrying cores. Always check the maker's data, and use a thicker cord for a long lead.

head: Conductor size
Typical rating
Typical use
rows: 18 AWG (about 0.8 mm²)
Lamps, small appliances
16 AWG (about 1.3 mm²)
Fans, light tools, short light-duty leads
14 AWG (about 2.1 mm²)
15 to 18 A
Heaters, kettles, heavy tools, general extension leads
12 AWG (about 3.3 mm²)
20 to 25 A
Heavy 110 V tools, long leads, 220 V machines
10 AWG (about 5.3 mm²)
25 to 30 A
Large 220 V portable machines

ol: **How much current?** I = P ÷ V from the nameplate. The cord's rating must be above it.
**Class I or Class II?** Three cores with an earth for a metal-bodied Class I appliance; two cores for Class II.
**What will it meet?** Heat (heater cord), oil and wear (rubber, OO types), rain and sun (W types), dragging on site (heavy-duty rubber).

**How long?** Just long enough to reach the work without strain and without an extension lead. Extra length adds voltage drop, tangles and trip hazards; too short, and the cord pulls on its terminals.
**Does it fit?** The cord must fit the appliance's entry bush and cord grip, and its cores must fit the terminals.

blocks.note: Replace like for like or better. If the maker fitted a 14 AWG three-core rubber cord, a thinner or PVC cord is not a repair. A thin cord on a heater overheats along its whole length, where nobody is looking.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Pattern
Rating
Blades
Typical use
rows: NEMA 1-15
110 V, 15 A, two-pin
Two flat parallel blades; on a **polarised** plug the neutral blade is wider
Class II appliances and lamps
NEMA 5-15
110 V, 15 A, earthed
Two flat parallel blades and a round earth pin
Most 110 V appliances and tools
NEMA 5-20
110 V, 20 A, earthed
One blade turned sideways, and an earth pin
Heavy 110 V appliances and tools
NEMA 6-15 and 6-20
220 V, 15 A or 20 A, earthed
Two blades in line (6-15), or one turned (6-20), and an earth pin
220 V air-conditioners, compressors, machines
NEMA 6-30 and 6-50
220 V, 30 A or 50 A, earthed
Larger blades
Large machines and welders
NEMA 14-30 and 14-50
110/220 V, 30 A or 50 A, four-pin
Two lines, a neutral and an earth
Dryers and cookers
Locking types (L prefix)
Various
Curved blades that twist and lock
Generators, machines and leads that must not pull out

ul: Fit the plug that matches the **nameplate voltage and current** and the outlet's rating. Never fit a 110 V plug to a 220 V appliance, or the other way round, to suit a spare outlet.
As a rule under the NEC-based code, a plug-connected load should be no more than **80%** of the outlet's rating: 12 A on a 15 A outlet, 16 A on a 20 A outlet, 24 A on a 30 A outlet.
The **earth pin is longer** than the blades, so the earth connects first and disconnects last.

On a polarised or earthed plug the terminals are colour-coded: **brass** screw for line, **silver** screw for neutral, **green** screw for earth. Line must go to the brass terminal so that switches and fuses in the appliance are in the line.
Equipment from Britain or Europe may arrive with a plug that does not fit Jamaican outlets. Fit the correct plug for its voltage; do not rely on a travel adaptor.

blocks.h: Three kinds of plug and cord

head: Type
Good points
Dealing with damage
rows: Re-wireable plug
Can be opened, inspected and refitted
Its quality depends on whoever wired it. If cracked or burnt, fit a new one and cut the cord back to sound cable.
Moulded-on plug
Sealed at the factory: reliable, cannot be wired wrongly
It cannot be opened or re-used. Cut it off, **destroy it at once**, and fit a re-wireable plug or a new cord.
Detachable cord set
Plug at one end, appliance connector at the other; changed without opening the appliance
Replace the whole set with one of the same type and rating. Never repair it.

blocks.note: A cut-off moulded plug with a stub of cord is deadly: if anyone pushes it into an outlet, the bare cut ends are live. Bend or cut off its blades and put it in the bin as soon as it is cut off.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Connector
Rating
Use
rows: C13 (fits a C14 inlet)
Usually 10 A; for cold appliances only
Computers, monitors, printers
C15 (like a C13, with a notch)
10 A; for hot appliances, up to 120 °C at the pins
Kettles, cookers, rice cookers. A C13 will not fit a C16 hot inlet, on purpose.
C19 (fits a C20 inlet)
Servers, large UPS units, some heaters
C7 ('figure of eight')
2.5 A, two-pin, no earth
Radios, small Class II equipment
C5 ('cloverleaf')
2.5 A, earthed
Laptop power supplies

ul: A damaged cord is **replaced whole**. Taped joints pull apart, overheat and expose live copper.
If two cords must be joined, use a **cord connector** (a plug and socket pair) of the right rating. The **socket half goes on the supply side**, so that no live pins are ever exposed.
A lead with a plug at both ends must never be made: its free plug has live pins.

flow: Record how the old cord was connected (photo)
Remove the old cord; destroy a cut-off plug
Strip the sheath only as far as needed
Cut the cores to length: earth longest
Strip each core to suit its terminal
Connect earth, neutral and line to the right terminals
Clamp the sheath in the cord grip
Check, then refit the cover

head: Point
Standard
Why
rows: Sheath
Stripped with a sheath stripper, without nicking the core insulation. The sheath must reach **inside the cord grip**.
Nicked insulation fails later. If only the cores are gripped, a tug pulls them off their terminals.
Earth core
Left **slightly longer** than line and neutral, with a little slack
If the cord is dragged out, the earth is the last to pull free, so the body stays earthed while the line is still connected.
Stripping the cores
Just enough for the terminal; no strands cut
Cut strands reduce the conductor's size and it runs hot.
Strands
Twisted neatly, all inside the terminal, no whiskers
A stray strand can touch another terminal or the case.
Bare conductor
None showing outside the terminal: the insulation reaches the terminal
Exposed copper can short or be touched.
Solder
Do **not** tin ends that go under a screw
Solder slowly creeps under pressure, so the screw loosens and the joint overheats.
Ferrules
A crimped bootlace ferrule of the right size may be used where the terminal is a clamp type that accepts it
It holds every strand together under the clamp.
Binding-screw terminals
Form a hook and place it **clockwise** round the screw
Tightening the screw then pulls the strands in, not out.
Tightness
Firm, to the maker's torque where given; tug each core gently
Loose terminals heat up, brown the plug and can start a fire.
Cord grip
Clamped on the sheath, firmly but without crushing it
The grip takes the strain, never the terminals.

blocks.h: If the grip does not fit

blocks.p: If the cord grip is too big for a thin cord, use the grip insert supplied with the plug, a plug made for that cord, or the right cord. Never knot the cord inside the plug, pad it with tape, or tighten the grip onto the cores.

ul: The cord enters through a smooth **bush or grommet**, never a bare hole in sheet metal. Many appliances have a **flex guard** (a tapered sleeve) that stops the cord bending sharply at the entry: refit it or fit a new one.
The appliance's own **cord grip** clamps the sheath.
Route the cores away from elements, hot surfaces and moving parts, and use the maker's clips and heat-resistant sleeving.
Earth to the earth terminal on the metal body; line to the switch or fuse side, as the old connection and the diagram show.
Crimped ring or spade terminals are made with the right crimp tool for that terminal size, and tugged to test them.

head: Item
Points to watch
rows: Portable machine (compressor, saw, mixer)
Heavy-duty rubber cord; plug to suit the nameplate voltage and current and the outlet; check for a motor capacitor before touching terminals.
Cord switch or machine switch
Must break the **line**. A switch wired into the neutral stops the machine but leaves its parts live when it is off.
Pendant light
The cord grips in the ceiling rose and lamp holder take the weight, not the terminals. A cord can carry only a light fitting; heavier ones hang on a chain or rod.
Lamp with a screw (Edison) holder
Line to the centre contact, neutral to the screw shell, using a polarised plug.
Metal lamp base or fitting
A bush or grommet where the cord passes through metal; earth connected if it is Class I.

head: To find
Formula
Example
rows: Current of an appliance
I = P ÷ V
Largest load a cord can supply
P = V × I
Resistance of a lead (both cores)
R = 2 × L × r
Voltage drop in a lead
VD = I × R
Voltage drop as a percentage
VD ÷ supply voltage × 100
Cords from a drum
Drum length ÷ cord length
100 m ÷ 3 m = 33 cords, with 1 m left over

blocks.p: The current goes out along one core and back along the other, so the length is counted **twice**. Typical resistances for one copper core are about 0.0132 Ω per metre for 16 AWG, 0.0083 for 14 AWG and 0.0052 for 12 AWG.

The same lead loses the same number of volts on 110 V as on 220 V for the same current, but on 110 V that is **twice the percentage**. A long lead on 110 V makes motors run hot and slow, and makes heaters weak. A common aim is to keep the drop below about 5%: use a shorter lead, a thicker lead or a nearer outlet.

blocks.note: Check both things for every lead: the **current rating** (will it overheat?) and the **voltage drop** (will the tool get enough voltage?). A long thin lead can pass the first and fail the second.
blocks.label: Tip

ol: Choose three-core heavy-duty rubber cord rated above the largest load, as short as the job allows.
Fit the **plug at the supply end** and a socket, or a weatherproof connector box, at the far end.
Clamp the sheath in the cord grip at both ends, with the earth core longest.
Test: earth continuity end to end, each core's continuity while flexing the cord, insulation resistance, and polarity at the socket.
Label it with its ID, the test date and your name, and enter it in the register.

head: Hazard
Why it matters
Control
rows: Coiled reel
A wound cable cannot lose its heat and can melt. Reel labels usually give two ratings: one fully unwound and a much lower one wound.
Unwind the reel fully for any heavy load.
Overloading
The currents of everything plugged into one lead add together.
Add up the loads; one heavy appliance per lead; no adaptors on adaptors.
Leads joined end to end
More resistance, more voltage drop, more connectors to fail.
Use one lead of the right length and size.
Wet ground
Water in a connector gives shock and tripping.
Outdoor-rated cord and weatherproof connectors, raised off the ground; **GFCI protection at the supply end**.
Crushing and hidden runs
A cord under a carpet, through a closed door or under furniture is damaged, or overheats, unseen.
Route leads in the open, protected by cable covers where people or vehicles cross.
Pulling by the cord
Strains the terminals and breaks strands inside.
Hold the plug to unplug.

blocks.note: An extension lead is a temporary supply. If a workshop or office uses leads every day to reach its machines, the right answer is more outlets, properly installed.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Every cord and plug you fit is inspected and tested before it is used. The same inspection and tests are used to check equipment already in service; in workplaces this is often called **portable appliance testing (PAT)**.

blocks.h: Visual inspection: most faults are found here

head: Part
Fail it if you find
rows: Cord
Coloured cores showing through the sheath, cuts, crushing, melted or hardened sections, taped joints, the wrong type or size for the appliance
Plug
Cracks, bent or loose pins, a missing earth pin, burn or brown marks, the wrong pattern for the appliance's voltage
Cord grips
Sheath not held at either end, grip loose or missing, cores taking the strain
Inside the plug
Wrong terminals, bare copper showing, stray strands, loose screws, tinned ends, earth core short or unconnected
Appliance
Cracked case, missing covers or guards, damaged switch, signs of overheating

blocks.p: Dirt, grease or a paint mark is cleaned off; it is not a reason to replace a cord. A plug that is **warm and browned at one pin** shows a loose connection in the plug or a worn outlet contact: check both.

head: Test
How
What it shows
Typical pass
rows: Earth continuity (Class I only)
Low-resistance ohmmeter from the plug's earth pin to the metal body, **flexing the cord** along its length
A fault current has a sound path back, so the breaker will trip
Very low and steady: commonly not more than about 0.1 Ω plus the resistance of the cord's earth core. A reading that jumps when the cord is flexed is a fail.
Core continuity and polarity
Ohmmeter from each plug pin to the core's far end or terminal
Each core is whole and on the right pin; the switch is in the line
Near 0 Ω on the right pair, open circuit to the others.
Insulation resistance
500 V DC tester between **line and neutral joined together** and earth (Class I), or the outside metal parts (Class II), with the appliance switch on
No leakage from the live parts to the body
Commonly at least 1 MΩ for Class I and 2 MΩ for Class II. Some heating appliances are allowed a lower figure (often about 0.3 MΩ); follow the maker and the Centre's test sheet.
Function test
Run on the protected test bench, by the instructor at the Centre
The appliance works and its controls and switch operate
Normal running, no heat, smell or sparking.

ul: A **Class II** appliance has no earth, so there is no earth continuity test.
**Reversed polarity** means line and neutral are swapped. The appliance may still work, but its switch and fuse are then in the neutral.
Keep your hands off the test leads and the appliance during the 500 V test, and warn others.
A high or unsteady earth reading: check the earth terminations at **both ends** first, then the cord.

head: Item
What it shows
rows: Pass label
The appliance ID, the test date, who tested it and when the next test is due, so users can see it has been checked.
Fail label
'Do not use', the fault and the date. The item is taken out of use at once and kept apart until repaired or scrapped.
Appliance register
For each item: ID, description, class, location, test dates and results, repairs, and the next due date.
Job record
Cord type and size, plug fitted, test results, the price, and any advice given.

ul: Open the first plug each trainee wires and go through every point with them; then spot-check. Looking at the outside proves nothing.
Ask the trainee to explain why each step matters: why the earth is longer, why the grip holds the sheath.
Test every finished item before it is labelled. Have faults corrected by the trainee who made them, retest, and note it in the training record.

head: Common trainee fault
What it leads to
rows: Sheath stops short of the cord grip
The cores take the strain and pull off the terminals
Earth core cut the same length as, or shorter than, the others
The earth pulls out first, leaving a live appliance unearthed
Too much insulation stripped
Bare copper outside the terminal: shorts and shocks
Strands cut or loose
Overheating; a whisker touching another terminal
Line and neutral swapped
Reversed polarity: switch and fuse in the neutral
Cover screwed down on a trapped core
Insulation crushed, a fault waiting to happen

flow: List every appliance and lead in a register, each with an ID
Set how often each type is checked, by how hard it is used
Teach users a quick look before each use, and how to report
Formal inspection and tests, with dated labels
Failed items out of use: repair or scrap
Review the register for items that keep failing

blocks.p: Intervals are set by risk. Site tools and extension leads that are dragged about every day need checking far more often than a printer that never moves. As an example, a workshop might check portable tools every 3 months and office equipment every 12 to 24 months. To count the work: 40 items checked every 6 months is 80 inspections a year.

ul: Explain in plain words why a taped joint, a thin cord or the wrong plug is dangerous, and what you recommend.
Give the price before you start: cord, plug, labour, with GCT at the current rate, and get agreement.
If a customer asks for something unsafe, such as a longer, thinner cord on a heater, or a 110 V plug on a 220 V machine, explain the risk and offer the safe way.
Show the customer the old cord, then cut it up and dispose of it so that nobody re-uses it.
Tell them how to look after the cord: hold the plug to unplug, keep it away from heat, do not run it under carpets.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can make plug-connected equipment safe to work on, including capacitors.
I can tell Class I, Class II and Class III appliances apart and say what cord each needs.
I can describe how a flexible cord is built and why solid wire is never used.
I can choose a cord type for heat, oil, wear, weather and site use.
I can work out an appliance's current and choose a cord rated above it.
I can match a plug to the nameplate and the outlet, and apply the 80% rule.
I can explain why plug patterns must never be defeated.
I can deal correctly with re-wireable plugs, moulded plugs and detachable cord sets, and choose the right appliance connector.
I can prepare and terminate a cord to standard at both ends, with the earth longest and the sheath in the grip.
I can explain why ends under screws are not tinned, and how to hook a conductor round a binding screw.
I can work out a lead's resistance, voltage drop and percentage drop, and decide whether its length is acceptable.
I can make up, test and label a site extension lead, with the plug at the supply end.
I can inspect a cord and plug and carry out the right tests for Class I and Class II.
I can label, record and keep an appliance register.
I can check trainees' work, set up an inspection programme and advise a customer.

terms: Bush / grommet
A smooth ring fitted in a hole in metal to protect a cord passing through.
Class I
An appliance with an earthed metal body; needs a three-core cord.
Class II
A double-insulated appliance with no earth connection; marked with a square inside a square.
Cord connector
A plug and socket pair for joining two cords; the socket half goes on the supply side.
Cord grip
The clamp that holds the cord's sheath where it enters a plug or appliance; also called strain relief.
Cord set
A detachable cord with a plug at one end and an appliance connector at the other.
Flex guard
A tapered sleeve at the cord entry that stops the cord bending sharply.
Flexible cord
A cable with fine-stranded cores made to be bent in use.
Moulded plug
A plug sealed onto its cord at the factory; it cannot be opened or re-used.
PAT
Portable appliance testing: regular inspection and testing of plug-connected equipment.
Polarised plug
A two-pin plug with a wider neutral blade, so it fits the outlet only one way.
Reversed polarity
Line and neutral swapped at a plug or outlet.
Sheath
The outer covering of a cord, protecting the insulated cores.
Voltage drop
The volts lost along a lead: current × the resistance of both cores.

c1.title: Dryers at a Half Way Tree hair salon
c1.text: Ms Shanique Barrett runs a hair salon in Half Way Tree, St Andrew. She brings three items to the Centre's repair bench. A plastic-bodied hand dryer, marked with a square inside a square and rated 110 V, 1,500 W, has a cord that is cracked where it bends at the handle. A hood dryer with a painted steel body, rated 110 V, 1,100 W, has been fitted by someone with a thin two-core cord and a two-pin plug. A table lamp for the nail station has a metal screw-type (Edison) lamp holder and needs a new plug. Trainee Rochelle does the work, checked by trainee leader Omar.

c2.title: Leads for a beach wedding at Discovery Bay
c2.text: An events company is setting up a wedding on a lawn beside the sea at Discovery Bay, St Ann. The sound desk and lights draw 12 A at 110 V and stand 35 m from the nearest outlet, on the villa's verandah. The company's leads are three-core rubber cords: 14 AWG (0.0083 Ω per metre for each core) and 12 AWG (0.0052 Ω per metre). It also has a cable reel labelled '13 A fully unwound, 5 A wound'. The grass is damp from the sprinklers. Trainee leader Jermaine is helping the company's technician, Mr Lascelles Brown, to set up.

c3.title: A table saw in a Junction school workshop
c3.text: The woodwork shop at a high school in Junction, St Elizabeth, has a portable 220 V table saw rated 3,300 W. Its cord has been chafed through to the cores by years of being dragged across the concrete floor through sawdust and machine oil, and its plug is cracked. The shop has 220 V outlets rated 15 A and 20 A, of different patterns. Trainee leader Latoya supervises trainee Devon, who will fit the new cord and a re-wireable plug with binding-screw terminals.

c4.title: Three bench jobs in Port Antonio
c4.text: At a repair shop in Port Antonio, Portland, trainee leader Sasha-Gay has three jobs. An electric kettle with a detachable cord set has lost its cord; the customer has brought a computer lead that 'almost fits'. A metal-bodied toaster oven, kept in a damp store room since the last hurricane, has had a new three-core cord fitted by a trainee and is ready for testing. A plastic pedestal fan marked with a square inside a square has a new two-core cord.

c5.title: Housekeeping equipment at a Runaway Bay hotel
c5.text: A hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann, asks the Centre to inspect the housekeeping department's portable equipment: 12 vacuum cleaners and 6 extension leads that are used on every shift, and 10 items in the office such as printers and a laminator, which are rarely moved. There is no list of the equipment and nothing is labelled. Trainee leader Nicholas leads three trainees. On the first morning a trainee shows him a plug she has rewired on a vacuum cleaner: the sheath stops 10 mm short of the cord grip, and the grip is clamped onto the three cores.

questions.q: What is the right repair for the hand dryer's cracked cord?
o: Bind the cracked part tightly with insulating tape and return it
Fit a new three-core cord and join its earth core to the motor frame
Cut out the cracked part and join the two ends inside the handle
Fit a new two-core cord of the same rating, with its flex guard
questions.why: A damaged cord is replaced whole, never taped or joined. The dryer is Class II (square inside a square), so it takes a two-core cord and must not be given an earth. The flex guard stops the new cord bending sharply at the handle, which is what cracked the old one.

questions.q: The hand dryer draws 13.6 A. Using typical ratings of 10 A for 18 AWG, 13 A for 16 AWG and 15 to 18 A for 14 AWG, which cord should Rochelle choose?
o: 18 AWG, as the dryer is used only for a few minutes at a time
16 AWG, as 13 A is close enough to the dryer's current
14 AWG, the first size rated above the dryer's current
Any size, provided the cord is kept shorter than 2 m
questions.why: 1,500 ÷ 110 = 13.6 A, and the cord must be rated above the appliance's current. 16 AWG at 13 A is just under, so it would run warm all day in a busy salon. 14 AWG is the first size with a rating above 13.6 A; check that it suits the maker's entry and grip.

questions.q: What must be done about the hood dryer's cord?
o: Fit a three-core cord, earthed to the body, and a three-pin plug
Leave it, since the paint on the steel body acts as extra insulation too
Keep the two-core cord, but change the plug to a polarised type
Keep it, and stick a double-insulation label on the dryer's body
questions.why: A steel-bodied appliance is Class I: its safety depends on the body being earthed, so that a fault trips the breaker. With a two-core cord a fault would leave the body live. Paint is not insulation you can rely on, and a label does not make an appliance double insulated.

questions.q: Rochelle fits a polarised two-pin plug to the table lamp. To which blade should the core from the lamp holder's screw shell go, and why?
o: The narrow blade, so the shell is live and the lamp lights sooner
Either blade, because a lamp works the same both ways round
The narrow blade, because the shell carries the larger current
The wide blade, so the shell that fingers can touch is neutral
questions.why: The wide blade of a polarised plug is the neutral. The screw shell is easy to touch when changing a lamp, so it must be on the neutral, with the switched line on the small centre contact deep in the holder. The lamp would light either way, which is why this fault goes unnoticed.

questions.q: About what voltage drop would a single 35 m lead of 14 AWG give at 12 A?
o: About 3.5 V
About 7 V
About 14 V
About 0.7 V
questions.why: Both cores count: R = 2 × 35 × 0.0083 = 0.58 Ω. VD = 12 × 0.58 = about 7 V, which is over 6% of 110 V. 3.5 V is the answer for one core only.

questions.q: The 14 AWG lead would lose more than 6% of the 110 V supply. What is the best way to deal with this?
o: Use two 14 AWG leads joined end to end, to share the load
Use the 12 AWG lead, which drops about 4.4 V, or a nearer outlet
Accept it, because sound equipment is not affected by low voltage
Plug the desk into a 220 V outlet through an adaptor to make up the loss
questions.why: A thicker conductor has less resistance: 2 × 35 × 0.0052 = 0.36 Ω, and 12 × 0.36 = 4.4 V, about 4%. A nearer supply point also helps. Joining leads end to end adds resistance, and 110 V equipment must never be put on 220 V.

questions.q: Mr Brown wants to feed the 12 A load from the cable reel with most of the cable still wound on the drum. What should Jermaine tell him?
o: It is fine, as 12 A is below the reel's 13 A rating
It is fine if the reel is kept in the shade under the verandah
Wind on even more cable, so that the turns cool each other
Unwind it fully: wound, it is rated for only 5 A
questions.why: A wound cable cannot lose its heat, so its rating falls sharply: this reel carries 13 A only when fully unwound. At 12 A on the drum the inner turns can soften and melt, shorting the cores.

questions.q: The lead to the lights must be joined to a second lead halfway across the damp lawn. Which arrangement is safest?
o: In a weatherproof box off the grass, with a GFCI at the verandah
The plug and socket wrapped in a plastic bag and taped at both ends
The joint laid on a dry towel, with a GFCI at the lighting end
The two leads joined with connectors and tape, then buried under the turf
questions.why: Water in a connector causes shock and tripping, so the joint goes in a weatherproof connector box, off the ground. A GFCI protects only what is connected after it, so it must be at the supply end to cover both leads. Bags trap water, and taped or buried joints are never acceptable.

questions.q: Which plug and outlet should the saw use?
o: The 15 A, 220 V pattern, since the saw draws exactly 15 A
A 110 V plug, so the saw can be used at any outlet in the shop
The 20 A, 220 V pattern, as 15 A is over 80% of 15 A
Whichever 220 V plug is in stock, as both patterns carry 220 V
questions.why: 3,300 ÷ 220 = 15 A. A plug-connected load should not exceed 80% of the outlet's rating: 12 A for a 15 A outlet, 16 A for a 20 A outlet. So the saw needs the 20 A pattern. A 110 V plug on a 220 V machine defeats the pattern that keeps voltages apart.

questions.q: Which cord is the best choice for the saw?
o: Three-core light PVC cord, because it is the easiest to strip
Three-core heavy-duty rubber cord with an oil-resistant sheath
Two-core parallel cord, because the saw has a plastic switch box
Single-core building wires drawn into a length of garden hose
questions.why: The saw is a metal-bodied machine, so it needs three cores with an earth. Its cord is dragged over concrete through sawdust and oil, which is what destroyed the old one, so it needs a thick rubber sheath that resists wear and oil. Solid building wire cracks when flexed.

questions.q: Devon forms each stripped core into a hook and puts it anticlockwise round its binding screw. Why does Latoya make him redo it?
o: Tightening the screw pushes an anticlockwise hook out
An anticlockwise hook reverses the polarity of the line and neutral
The screw cannot be tightened to full torque on an anticlockwise hook
Anticlockwise hooks are only allowed on the earth terminal's green screw
questions.why: The screw turns clockwise as it tightens. A hook laid clockwise is drawn in under the head; one laid the other way is pushed open and squeezed out, leaving a loose joint with stray strands. Polarity depends on which terminal a core is on, not on the direction of the hook.

questions.q: For the saw's own terminal block, which has screw-clamp terminals, how should the fine-stranded ends be prepared?
o: Twisted, then coated with solder so that the strands stay together
Folded back over the insulation, so that the clamp grips both
Trimmed down by a few strands, so that they enter the clamp easily
Twisted, then fitted with crimped ferrules of the right size
questions.why: A crimped ferrule holds every strand under the clamp. Solder creeps under pressure, so the clamp loosens and the joint overheats; cutting strands off reduces the conductor's size; and clamping onto insulation gives a poor, loose contact.

questions.q: What should Sasha-Gay do about the kettle's missing cord set?
o: Use the computer lead, filing its connector until it fits the kettle
Supply a hot-appliance cord set (C15) of the kettle's rating
Fit the computer lead, as both connectors are rated at 10 A
Wire a cord directly to the kettle's inlet pins and tape them
questions.why: A kettle's inlet gets hot, so it takes the notched hot-condition connector, rated for 120 °C at the pins. A computer lead's C13 connector is for cold appliances only and is shaped so that it will not fit: forcing it defeats that protection.

questions.q: On the toaster oven, the reading from the plug's earth pin to the body jumps between 0.08 Ω and 1.9 Ω as the cord is flexed near the plug. What does this show?
o: A pass, because the lowest reading is the one that counts
A weak battery in the ohmmeter, so the test can be ignored
A loose or broken earth connection at the plug end: a fail
Normal behaviour, as all cords read higher when they are bent
questions.why: A sound earth path reads low and steady however the cord is moved. A reading that jumps when the cord is flexed means broken strands or a loose termination, here near the plug. The earth could be open just when a fault happens, so the item fails until it is re-terminated and retested.

questions.q: After the earth is put right, the toaster oven's insulation resistance from line and neutral joined to the body reads 0.05 MΩ. What should Sasha-Gay do?
o: Pass it, since any reading above zero shows there is no short
Pass it, but tell the customer to use it only on a dry day
Disconnect the earth core, so that the leakage cannot trip a GFCI
Fail it for now: find the cause, such as damp, and retest
questions.why: 0.05 MΩ is far below even the lower figure allowed for heating appliances, so current is leaking from the live parts to the body. Damp storage may have let the elements absorb moisture. It is not returned until the cause is found and dealt with as the maker advises and the reading is acceptable. Removing the earth would hide the fault and make it deadly.

questions.q: Which set of checks is right for the pedestal fan?
o: Visual check, polarity, insulation resistance; no earth test
Earth continuity from the plug to the plastic body, then insulation
Earth continuity only, as plastic bodies need no insulation test
A function test only, as a double-insulated fan cannot be tested
questions.why: A Class II appliance has no earth conductor, so there is nothing for an earth continuity test to measure. It still gets a full visual inspection, a check that the cores are on the right pins, and an insulation resistance test as the maker advises, before the function test.

questions.q: What should Nicholas have the trainee do about the vacuum cleaner plug?
o: Tighten the grip harder on the cores, so that they cannot move
Wrap tape round the cores to thicken them, then clamp the grip
Remake the end so the grip clamps the sheath, then test it
Leave it, as the terminal screws are tight and will hold the cores
questions.why: The cord grip must hold the sheath. Clamped on the cores, it crushes their insulation and every tug on the cord goes onto the cores and their terminals. The trainee strips the end again to the right lengths, with the earth longest, and the plug is tested before it is labelled.

questions.q: How should Nicholas set the inspection intervals for the hotel's equipment?
o: The same for all, so that the register is simple to keep
Vacuum cleaners and leads more often than office items
Office items most often, as they cost the most to replace
Only when a member of staff reports that something has failed
questions.why: Intervals follow risk. Equipment that is moved, dragged and plugged in on every shift is damaged far sooner than a printer that sits still, so it is checked more often. Waiting for a failure report means waiting for a shock or a fire.

questions.q: One vacuum cleaner fails its inspection: its cord has two taped joints. What should happen to it?
o: Label it 'Do not use', remove it, record it, replace the cord
Fit a pass label with a note asking staff to handle it with care
Leave it in service until the end of the week, then repair it
Put it back on the shelf unlabelled, at the back, to be dealt with later
questions.why: A failed item must not be usable by mistake. It is labelled, taken out of service at once and kept apart, the register records the fault and the action, and it returns only after the whole cord is replaced and it passes its tests.

questions.q: A customer's house has old two-slot outlets with no earth. He asks you to cut the earth pin off his new steel-bodied fridge's plug so that it fits. What is the best advice?
o: Cut the pin off, as fridges rarely develop faults to the case
Fit a two-pin plug and connect the earth core to the neutral pin
Use a two-pin adaptor and leave its earth tag unconnected
Keep the plug whole and have an earthed outlet installed
questions.why: A steel-bodied fridge is Class I and depends on its earth: without it, a fault can leave the case live with nothing to trip the breaker. The safe answer is an earthed outlet, properly installed. Joining earth to neutral can make the case live if the neutral fails.
